speechtext: If there was no railroading, why were the}' taken to Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was done to suit the convenience of the department and its officials. The board is not being held for an isolated case; probably half a dozen cases will be heard. One of the reasons for its being held in Halifax is because the ships sail from that port.
It is very hard on the men charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I grant you. A crime
charged against a man is investigated in that man's province; that is, when we are speaking of criminal charges. These men may not be charged with any criminal offence; possibly they will not.
All the worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But if they are here in
breach of the provisions of our law, they may be deported. They may be thoroughly undesirable people, and as such they are liable to deportation. There may be no charge of a criminal nature in connection with them.

That makes it all the
worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: ' But the law is there, and if it is there it should be enforced. The way to get rid of a bad law is to enforce it.

If the law
can be enforced to any such wild extremes as this, I have never before heard of anything of the kind being done. Will the minister give me some illustrations ? I have already cited to the committee cases in which I was personally interested and affected, and in which the investigation took place in the province concerned. I cannot understand the minister's point of view.

I quite realize that the Minister of Justice is not the responsible minister, and also that it is unsafe to become too much excited over newspaper reports. But at the moment, until we have other information, we can proceed only on the assumption that there is some foundation of fact in the statements that have appeared, coupled with the telegram which has been received. During the last ten years, while I have been a member, I have been endeavouring to instil into people from other lands who are in my province and in my riding, those principles which I consider to be sound, of the Canadian spirit, the British institutions which I have always
felt were fine, noble, the best we have in this imperfect world. In particular I have been holding them up in comparison with the customs in other lands and the ideas of men who come from other countries, and have been doing my best to make of these men real Canadians. One of the things I have always held up has been just that which has been cited, that any man in this country, whether a citizen by birth or naturalization or simply a resident who has come within our borders, is assured, no matter who he is or what he has done, of fair treatment and a fair chance. I am not defending those men; I do not know them. If they have done anything wrong- and I assume they may have-I am the last man to condone the wrong, any more than I would condone a murder or approve any crime. But I would also be the last man to stand by and see even a murderer lynched or hurried to conviction without a fair trial. Where a man is charged with commission of a crime if the accused cannot provide counsel or has no funds, the court, in its meticulous care that British justice be upheld, will furnish counsel for him. If what has happened is as has been stated, the minister is right in saying that no law has been broken, but he is not right when he says that in doing that, they were simply obeying the law. There is a great difference between obeying the law-that is in doing something that the law commands-and simply staying within the limits of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I referred to the actions of the mounted police.

Quite so. I make no criticism of the police themselves. They were acting under orders and had no option but to do as they were told; the better policemen they were, the more meticulously would they obey orders, whether they were right or wrong. I am speaking of the authority under which they acted. The minister did not refer to the police obeying the law; he referred to the Minister of Immigration obeying the law. The Minister of Immigration certainly acted within the law; he did not do anything against the law, but the law did not force him to do as he did. It gave him or his department discretion as to where the trials should take place and what action should be taken. The discretion has been within the law. The law itself my be all right, yet good law may be abused. Actions may be within the law but still be not fair or equitable.
I am chiefly interested from this one aspect, that of the effect which the report of such action, if true or if left uncontradicted, will have upon people from other countries among
2fi96
Supply-Justice-R.C.M.P.

whom I, with others, have been working in an endeavour to clear from their minds soviet, bolshevist conceptions and make them good Canadians. I have assured them that no matter how poor they might be in this world's goods, no matter how ignorant they might be or to what extent they were unacquainted with our language or our customs, once they came into this country they would receive the same treatment and be accorded the same justice as the richest British-born that could come into the land. If action has been taken as has been stated, and if it goes without contradiction, what can I say to those men? They know, and everybody in this house knows, that no educated man of influential family, of position, of wealth, with influential friends, would be treated in such a way. We know that; they all know that. If other men are treated differently, then all that has been said by many of us, doing our best to stem the tide of faulty opinions and principles, is of no avail. The work we are doing has been hampered; our high ideals have been swept overboard. It is true the minister is not the one responsible, but in the eyes of the world what is he? He is the Minister of Justice; he and his department represent justice in this land. I would appeal to him, in his capacity as the dispenser of justice in Canada, to see that justice is done in this case.

May I submit just one or two other considerations? As I understand the matter, the Immigration Act is designed to state what class of people shall come into this country, and to give the minister power to deal with any individuals belonging to prohibited classes that have got by and that should be deported because they are unfit to be immigrants. Clause 41 of the Immigration Act gives a list of certain persons to be deemed to belong to the prohibited or undesirable classes. It is intended to keep that class of people out of the country, but I submit that this law was never designed or should never be used to try people for crimes after they have been for a considerable period in Canada. One of these men, according to my information, has been twenty years in this country. He ought not to come under the jurisdiction of the immigration authorities. He has been here long enough to establish a certain domicile.

He should be
naturalized.

For my purpose it does not make any difference whether he is naturalized or not. He has been here long 
enough to establish a certain residence, and he ought not to come under the Immigration Act. If he has committed any offence against the criminal code, by all means let him be tried, Convicted and deported if we can deport him. I am not arguing against deportation for cause; but let him have a trial; let us not use the Immigration Act, which is designed to keep certain people out of the country, as a means of putting them out. That is not a fair way of dealing with the situation. It is quite true that a man may get inside the gate in some surreptitious way, and it may be found after he has been here a year or two that he has made false representations, or was not what he represented himself to be. The Immigration Act is designed to take care of people of this class and provide for their being sent back if they have been here a month or two or a year or so, but when a man has been here for a number of years it seems to me that he ought to come under our regular procedure. The very next clause of the Immigration Act, clause 42, says that the minister-
-may order such person to be taken into custody and detained at an immigration station for examination and an investigation of the facts alleged in the said complaint to be made by a board of inquiry or by an officer acting as such.
That means that if he comes in by way of Halifax he will be detained at Halifax and examined there by a board, but it certainly does not mean that after a man has come to this country and has lived for twenty years in Winnipeg he is to be taken back and examined at an immigration station at Halifax. There is no authority in the act whatever for such a procedure as that, none whatsoever. If he has to be detained at an immigration station there is an immigration station at Winnipeg where he might have been detained.
Further than that, in the case of one of these men, he has a Canadian bom wife and a Canadian born child in Canada. Now what does the act say with regard to them? Subsection 6 of section 42 says:
In any case where deportation of the head of a family is ordered, all dependent members of the family may be deported at the same time; and in any case where deportation of a dependent member of a family is ordered on account of having become a public charge, and in the opinion of the minister such circumstance is due to wilful neglect or non-support by the head or other members of the family morally bound ito support such dependent member, then all members of the family may be deported at the same time.
I presume that this section means that this Canadian born woman with her Canadian born child may be summarily deported to Poland or Russia or Germany, or from whatever country

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
this man may have come. If he is not deported with his wife, it means that she and her child are to be left in Canada and her husband sent overseas-a family absolutely broken up. Those members of the house who a few years ago objected so strongly to divorce, might I think, very well have something to say about a forcible divorce of that kind, where the head of the family is taken away and the dependent wife and family are left in this country.
Further, the minister says that every opportunity will be given for appeal. Let me read the notice to be sent to the person ordered to be deported:
If you claim to be a Canadian citizen or to have acquired Canadian domicile, you have the right to consult counsel and appeal to the courts against deportation.
These people, I believe, are not naturalized, hence they do not come under the first paragraph of this section. I go on:
In all other cases you may appeal to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization against any decision of the board of inquiry or officer in charge whereby you are ordered to be deported unless such decision is based upon a certificate of the examining medical officer that you are affected with a loathsome disease or a disease which may become dangerous to the public health. The formal notice of appeal will be supplied to you by the immigration officer in charge upon request and upon deposit of the sum of twenty dollars for the cost of your maintenance and the sum of ten dollars for the maintenance of each person dependent upon you until the minister has decided upon your case.
It is that second part of the section which applies to these particular people, and unless they can produce the twenty dollars and the ten dollars for each dependent they have no chance even for an appeal. That is a very serious state of affairs. You take a man quickly away from where he lives without giving him any opportunity to obtain ready cash, and move him two thousand miles from where his friends are located, and it is almost impossible for him to make an appeal to the minister. The result is that he is clapped on board ship and is on his way across the Atlantic without even a -chance for an appeal. I know that the Minister of Justice cannot think that that is a fair sort of trial. He must realize that an appeal of that kind is a mere sham. I would urge upon him, as Minister of Justice and as a member of the government, to see to it that these -people, whatever their crimes may be, are given a fair trial in Canada.

I should like to ask a question concerning a condition existing in one of the reserves in Manitoba. Perhaps the minister may be in a better position to answer if I state the circumstances. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Any goods bought by the Indian department through properly appointed and qualified officials will be paid for by the department. But as to accounts incurred with a dealer by individual Indians the department does not hold itself responsible for payment. There was a practice, which to some extent has been discontinued, whereby an Indian agent would sign an order or agree that a merchant might charge to an Indian certain goods and he, the agent, out of the proceeds of the Indian's crop would endeavour to pay the merchant. I believe a difficulty has arisen in the particular case to which the hon. member for Macdonald has referred. I may say representations have been made to the department with regard to accounts owing to merchants and dealers by Indians in the Swan Lake area. Some of the accounts have been submitted to me to dhow that the goods were charged and in most instances the accounts bore the signature of the farm instructor. It may be that the Indians themselves requested the agent to purchase the flour for them out of this fund rather than have it all distributed to them in cash. Apparently-and I use the word because the department issued no instructions to the agent with regard to it-he asked for quota-

tions from different firms to supply this flour. Whether he has placed an order with any firm, as I have told the hon. member, I have no information to give him.

How is the grain or
wheat from these Indian reserves sold? Some of the larger milling companies have stated that they are sometimes in a position to give a better price than the department obtain, and yet they are never given an opportunity of bidding.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Indian agent, as the hon. member knows, does practically all the business for the Indians under his charge. One of his duties is to see that the Indians' grain is sold to the best advantage, and I presume he sells it to the elevator companies at the best price obtainable.

It sometimes happens
that the milling companies are able to give a better price for the wheat than are the regular grain dealers, but the larger companies have stated that they never get an opportunity to buy.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That business is not transacted departmentally, and I am informed that the agent does not report to the department as to whom he sells the wheat or what price he obtains for it, although, as I stated a few moments ago, his duty is to see that the wheat is sold to the best advantage in order that the individual Indian may receive the most for his crop.

Is the minister able to give
the name of the medical officer who looks after the needs of the Indians of the Chapel Island reserve in the county of Richmond, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will endeavour to give
the hon. member an answer in a moment. I observe that the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) is now in his seat. On May 2 he asked that certain information be brought before the committee in regard to the purchase of coal for certain agencies in Alberta. I am now in a position to inform the committee that in 1930-31, agent Gooderham secured quotations for the fuel requirements of Namaka, Gleichen and Cluny from William McConnell, of Gleichen, and the Midland Coal Company of Drumheller. In that year coal was purchased from Mr. McConnell, who submitted the lowest tender, at the following prices: $7.50 per ton, f.o.b. agency; $8.50 per ton, f.o.b. farm No. 3; $9.50 per ton, f.o.b. farm B. In 1930-31, coal was purchased again from William McConnell, he having submitted

Supply-Indian Affairs
the lowest prices, at the following figure; $7.50 per ton, f.o.b. agency; $7.50 per ton, f.o.b. farm No. 2; $8.50 per ton, f.o.b. farm No. 3; S9.10 per ton, f.o.b. farm A; $9.50 per ton, f.o.b. farm B. Here I desire to draw to the attention of the hon. member and of the committee the fact that the answer given to a question asked by the hon. member for Bow River was incorrect, as the official of the department who compiled the figures gave the amounts of the highest tender for the year 1932-33 instead of the figures of the lowest tender, an error which I now correct.

Has the minister the
names of the other persons who were asked to tender, with the amounts of their tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have given the hon.
member the names of those who were asked to tender.
Was only Mr. McConnell asked to tender?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly the hon. gentleman did not hear me. A few moments ago I said that the Midland collieries of Drum-heller were also asked to tender.

Were they
asked to tender in 1931-32 also?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And who
else?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is all, just the two.

What was the tender
of the Midland Coal Company of Drumheller?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For the year 1930-31 the
figures were as follows:
	McConnell	Midland
Agency	.. $7 50	$7 65Farm A	. . 9 50	9 65Farm No. 3.. . .	. . 8 50	9 101931-32	Agency	.. $7 50	$7 65Farm No. 2.. . .	.. 7 50	7 65Farm A	.. 9 10	9 25Farm 13	. . 9 50	9 65Farm No. 3.. ..	. . 8 50	8 65
On May 2, when these estimates were being considered, the hon. member for Bow River asked the following question:
Mr. Garland (Bow River): Since the mine is producing 3,085 tons of coal, and, as the minister states, he hopes to produce a greater quantity next year, why is his department purchasing coal from outside at more than twice the amount? Is that economic? Is it common sense? If the Canadian National Railway system was run on that basis it. would be broke long ago.
To which I made the following answer:
Mr. Murphy: As I stated, the mine has been open only a few months, and it may be that the department was not in a position at the time-I speak again subject to correction-to supply its needs. In other words, the tenders were called for for the season 1931-32, prior to the opening of the mine. But now that we are in a position to meet those requirements, there is no reason why the coal [DOT]should not be supplied to the agency from the mine provided it is suitable coal for their requirements.
I asked my officials to wire the agent Yflg why tenders had been asked for when Hi had a coal mine of our own, in order to see if I was generally correct in my statement, and the following telegram was sent:
Question raised in house as to why department did not use coal mined from reserve for agency purposes instead of purchasing by tender. Is Blackfoot coal not suitable for agency pur- , poses? If it is, can it be used in the future? Explain fully. Rush reply.
To this the following answer was received:
A. S. Williams,	_
Acting Superintendent General Indian Affairs, Ottawa.
Tenders for agency coal awarded last August. Blackfoot coal mine not open until October. Coal from Blackfoot suitable and could be used in future if mine under supervision. Without supervisor we cannot rely on supplies.
G. H. Gooder.
I think I was generally correct in the statement I made in the house on May 2, when I said this mine was not in active operation when the agent asked for tenders for this coal. It is true that in answer to a question by the hon. member for Bow River certain figures were given showing that a certain amount of money had been spent on that mine in the two previous years. I may explain that that money was spent in the purchase of tools for the operation of the mine, and that active mining operations as such had not been carried on, the Indians simply doing a certain amount of drift mining in that area.

There is still something to be explained in connection with this matter. The quotations mentioned by the minister, running from $7.50 for the year 1931-32, are still $1.10 higher than the tenders received by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for only twelve tons of coal delivered at the barracks. Here is evidence that $1.10 more was paid than the coal could have been procured for if tenders had been called for by advertisement. That will require some explanation. With regard to the coal mine on the reserve, that mine has been open and in operation for some four years. In 1929 the mine produced 260 tons; in 1930 it produced
Supply-Indian Affairs

600 tons, or twice the requirements of the agency, and in 1931 it produced 3,085 tons. The minister explains the fact that the agency invited tenders-of course from certain selected individuals-in August last by the statement that coal was not being supplied by the mine on the reserve. The minister says that at -that time the mine on the reserve was not open and operating, but may I submit to the minister that the Midland coal mine was not open at the time either? Most of the domestic coal mines in Alberta are closed during the summer months, and in all probability at the time tenders were called for most of the mines in the Drumheller valley were not operating. The department must have had knowledge that this mine in the reserve would be producing approximately 3,000 tons that year, and it would know about the time it would require the coal. The Indians were available for labour, and in my opinion they could have supplied themselves from their own mines. When the minister is answering this question, I wish he would state if it is the general custom of the Department of Indian Affairs not to invite tenders by advertising but simply to invite one or two selected individuals to make a tender.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have now before me the answer given to the question asked by the hon. member for Bow River with regard to the production of this particular mine. As I stated a moment ago the production in 192930 was very limited, the Indians doing a certain amount of drift mining. As the department has no one in charge of that mine at all times, the figures given are only approximately correct. In 1929 there was mined 200 tons; in 1930, 600 tons and in 1931, 3,085 tons. The wire from the agent which I quoted a moment ago shows that this mine was not operating this year until about October. Prior to that time the agent had called for tenders to cover the requirements of the reserve, not for individual Indians particularly but for the agency buildings.
On whose authority?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think any particular instructions were given this year. The agent would simply carry out the practice he had followed in other years and at a certain time of the year ask for tenders.

When was the coal
delivered in 1931-32?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some bills are dated
January 5, 1931, for deliveries in December, 1930; some are dated February, 1931, for

delivery in January; some are dated March, 1931, for February deliveries. I have no bills for 1931 or 1932 showing deliveries last winter.

When were the tenders
called for the 1930-31 supply?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Tenders were called for
on August 29, 1931, and on September 26, 1930.

In the year when the
mine was likely to be operated by the agency, why were tenders asked for so much earlier than in the previous year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago,
no special instructions are sent out to agents with regard to the purchasing of supplies; these matters are in their hands and they carry on as a matter of business. The agent selects the time to ask for tenders.

Can the minister give
any information as to the business qualifications of this agent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that he is
considered to be one of the best agents we have. His father carried on the duties of Indian agent before him.

What kind of coal was
delivered in 1931-32, and from what mine?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Double screened lump
coal.
From what mine?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Neither the tender forms,
the abstract or the accounts give that information.
Has an Indian agent been appointed recently at Cacouna?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not received any advice of an appointment at that place.

Will the minister give me
an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The position at Chapel
island is vacant at present.
How long has it been vacant?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not certain as to the exact length of time, but I believe a matter of a few weeks.

The complaint which I received is that it has been vacant quite a while. I understand that this is because there is no Conservative doctor near the reserve If there is a Conservative doctor close to the reserve I have no objection to his being appointed at a time when the Conservative

Supply-Indian Affairs
party is in power, but if this position is being left vacant because there is no Conservative doctor near the reserve, then in the interests of the Indians a Liberal doctor should be appointed. My understanding is that this vacancy has existed for some months, in fact ever since a certain gentleman was appointed to the Senate. Previous to that time Senator Macdonald was the medical man in charge of this reserve, and in my opinion he was the proper man to have the job under a Conservative government, he being a good Conservative. The only other doctor there was the man who held the position before 1930, and who, no doubt quite properly, was discharged after this government came into power. It seems to me, if there is no Conservative doctor near, in the interests of the Indians, this other man should be reappointed immediately. I should like the minister to tell me exactly what the position is in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I anticipated that when I asked the hon. member to defer his question, I would have all the information that he desires. If he will kindly wait a little longer until I get another official here, I shall be able to give him fuller information. I have a certain general knowledge of the matter, but I desire to answer his question as accurately as possible, and I shall obtain the services of the other official as soon as I can.

It is not necessary to do that. I am quite satisfied with the minister's explanation as far as it went, and I want him also to take what I say. I said it in good faith and I think I was fair enough to say that if there was a Conservative doctor there, he should be appointed immediately. I understand there is not a Conservative doctor within a good many miles; therefore the only doctor there being a Liberal, he should be appointed without delay. The cost will not be very much, and rather than have the Indians suffer from want of medical attention, I think my hon. friend will agree with me, if my statement is correct, that doctor should be appointed immediately.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that the services are being performed at the present time by a doctor who is being paid on accounts, so the Indians are not suffering from lack of medical attention.
What doctor is that and where does he live?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Doctor Digout.
That is the man I should like to have appointed; he is a Grit.

There is another case of an Indian doctor in Shelburne county. Doctor L. P. Churchill was the Indian doctor there for a number of years and he was replaced comparatively recently by the appointment of Doctor C. A. Herbin. I asked the minister, early in the session, on whose recommendation the change was made. When the answer came down it was, according to page 389 of Hansard, "on instructions issued by the superintendent general." As reported on page 434 of Hansard, I pointed out that this was not an answer to the question, and I do not think I have had any answer since. I want to ask my hon. friend on whose recommendation the change was made.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The question as put by the hon. member, I think he will agree, was one based upon an assumption. It was not a direct question.
Well, I am asking the minister the question: was it made on a recommendation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my memory serves me correctly, yes.
On whose recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry that at the present moment I cannot recall, but I am quite willing to answer the question; I have no abjection to doing so.

I am sure of that. I only want to point out that it has not been answered. The question was, on whose recommendation the appointment was made, and the answer, "on instructions issued by the superintendent general," is not very informative nor, I think, is it a proper answer. I should like to indicate to the minister the situation with regard to this appointment. Doctor Churchill is an ex-service man, with, I think, three years' service overseas and the military cross. He was born in the county of Shelburne; he has lived there all his life. The gentleman who has replaced him, Doctor Herbin, has lived in the county some five years and has no overseas service. I want to ask the minister the reason for the dismissal of Doctor Churchill and the appointment of Doctor Herbin.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This position occupied
formerly by Doctor Churchill and later by Doctor Herbin is not one which carries a salary. The accounts are paid on what is know as the "call system;" that is, the agent calls in any doctor to provide the medical services for the Indians in question. It is not a regular salaried position.
Supply-Indian Affairs

I have not the answer yet. My question was: Why was it that Doctor Churchill's services were dispensed with and Doctor Herbin was appointed? To say that the position does not happen to be a salaried one is not any answer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think, if I may say so with all deference to my hon. friend, it is a proper answer. May I illustrate it in this way: My hon. friend in the course of his own private life may call in the services of a certain physician for his family at a particular time, and at a later date he may call in the services of another physician. Would he say, simply because he called in another doctor, that he dismissed the first one?
I asked simply why the change was made.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was not the original question. I think I answered that a few moment ago, when I said that the recommendation had been received by the minister.
What was the reason given for the recommendation? The minister does not act simply on a recommendation, without some reason being given for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I stated to the hon. gentleman that I was unable to recall who made the recommendation, but I fancy I carried out the practice which has been in vogue for many years, namely, that if a responsible minister receives a recommendation from a member of this house or from someone else in whom he has confidence, to do a certain thing, it is frequently done.
How frequently?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Most frequently, may I say, and I make no apologies for taking such action. If a colleague of mine in the government or a member in this house, whom I know personally and in whom I have confidence, makes a recommendation to me, then I am prepared to act upon his recommendation.
Will the minister make inquiries as to the increased expense to the country caused by accepting that recommendation, or will he accept it without such inquiry?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As possibly the hon. member is aware, the affairs of the Indian department will be administered this year for an amount some 81,800,000 less than two years ago.
That is no answer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman just contain himself for a moment? Not only in this case but in all similar cases throughout Canada instructions have been issued that those who are providing medical services for the Indians at various places must have their accounts kept to a minimum, and if I am not mistaken, a certain amount has been set which they must not exceed. I can assure the hon. member that those accounts, along with those for this particular doctor's services, will be very carefully examined and kept to a minimum.

The minister is not quite fair to himself or to the committee. Nobody asked for a long statement with regard to the general expenditures of the department. I asked a simple question. The minister stated that it was his practice, for which he made no apologies, to accept the recommendation of anyone in whom he had confidence with regard, generally speaking, to a change of office or the administration of his department. My simple question was whether he made any inquiry as to the relative expense which would result to the public from accepting that recommendation as compared with maintaining the position as it stood before the recommendation came in. I do not think there can be any misunderstanding about that question. It has nothing to do with the million dollars at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am quite willing to accept the lecture of my hon. friend as to the length and kind of answer I should give although I have not taken exception to the length or type of question which he has asked, and if my answer does not please him I can only express my regret. I am answering to the best of my ability and giving him the information which I thought he desired. I have nothing to withhold.
I am waiting for the answer, after all that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as I am aware, no particular inquiry was made in this instance as to whether the charge for the service would be increased or not. I gave the general answer which I thought would be more satisfactory to my hon. friend, that the expenses in this case as in all others would be kept to a minimum.

My hon. friend presumed to give the general practice and was laying down a rule which I have not heard stated before in this house. I was interested to know how it was that that practice applied and whether in applying it the minister makes any inquiry at all into the relative cost of accepting

Supply-Indian Affairs
the recommendation as compared with the cost before the recommendation was made. In this case no such inquiry was made, I understand. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I want to point out, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this appointment, that assuming one call is made on each Indian in the district during the year from the residences of these two men, it would cost this country, with Dr. Churchill making the calls, in view of his place of residence, S478 a year, whereas with the gentleman now appointed on this recommendation, and as I said before, not an ex-service man, it will cost $957 a year. In other words, there is an increase of nearly $500 in expenses to the department assuming that one call on each Indian is made during the year. That amounts to the statutory increase for the year of nearly seven or eight civil servants, which we found it impossible to give because of the fact that this country was so short of funds. I point out to my hon. friend now that, take it on any basis you like, the increased cost of administering his department in this case is one hundred per cent, if only one visit is made to each Indian during the year. The minister cannot justify this appointment on any ground, and if he has made other appointments on the same basis, one million dollars will be needed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member has stated that if such and such happens, the expenses of this particular service will be increased about one hundred per cent. I submit in all fairness that the hon member has no justification for making that statement. How he can inform the committee that the expenses of this particular service are going to be increased by some eight or nine hundred dollars this year passes my comprehension. I told him in my general answer a few moments ago that in a number of cases, if not in all- and if it has not been done in all cases it will be-instructions have been given by me that these services throughout Canada must not exceed a certain amount based upon the expenses that have been incurred in previous years. I thought in stating that I was giving the hon. member the information he desired. I was not seeking to evade his question at all.

The medical attendance
must be so and so and no more, whether the Indian dies or not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not what I said.
That is the only inference.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member may infer that but that is not what I said.
It is the only inference.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I submit differently. The service will be provided for these Indians as it has been in the past, but the expenses for the service must not exceed a certain amount per year.
How are you going to regulate it?

I will tell the minister how I arrived at the figure. It is quite simple. There are forty Indians in that county, and twenty-two of them live in the town of Shelburne, where Doctor Churchill lived. They would be called on at S3 a call, on the basis of my hon. friend's charge. Doctor Herbin lives at Lockeport, and a call from Lockeport on an Indian in Shelburne will cost $19, or at the rate of one dollar per mile. That is how the difference is made up. But my hon. friend is so keen to carry out this practice and accept recommendations, that he will displace an ex-service man who has given good service overseas and who has lived in the county all his life, in favour of a man who has lived there only five years and is not an ex-service man; and he will make that change without any inquiry as to the relative cost. In order to complete the comparison I will give my hon. friend a table of costs right straight through for visiting all the Indians living in Shelburne county who will be attended by this doctor.
Here is the return my hon. friend gave. I will give the number of Indians resident in each particular place, and the number of miles from Lockeport, and the number of miles from Shelburne. There are nine Indians at Barrington, thirty-six miles from Shelburne. One call on each Indian from Shelburne would be S324 a year. There are four Indians in Sable River, twenty-two miles from Shelburne. One call on each Indian would be $88 a year. There are twenty-two Indians in Shelburne town. At three dollars a call by Doctor Churchill, who lives in Shelburne, that would be $66 a year, or a total of $478 for Doctor Churchill to call on each Indian in the county once during the year. On the other hand, Doctor Herbin lives at Lockeport, away off from the largest number of Indians, who live at Shelburne. Lockeport is nineteen miles from Shelburne, where there are twenty-two Indians, and at a charge of one dollar per mile, for Doctor Herbin to call on these twenty-two Indians once during the year would cost $418. To call on the four
Supply-Indian Affairs

Indians at Sable River, eleven miles from Lockeport, would cost $44 a year. To call on the nine Indians at Barrington, fifty-five miles from Lockeport, would cost S495 a year, or a total of $957 for Doctor Herbin making one call during the year on each Indian. So I point out to my hon. friend that it is a pretty expensive practice that he has adopted of accepting recommendations from his colleagues or from people whom he considers responsible. Apart from the increased cost of administration I protest most vigorously against the replacement of a man of Doctor Churchill's standing in the community, and an ex-service man, by Doctor Herbin, who has been there a comparatively short time, and for no reason whatever so far as the minister has given any. But we can well imagine what the reason is, and it is costing this country a lot of money to carry out this parctice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Again may I point out
to the hon. member that he is basing his statement on figures which he himself has set up.

I beg my hon. friend's
pardon; I am basing my statement on figures in the minister's own return.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will please not interrupt; I did not interrupt him.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. It is that my hon. friend cannot make a misstatement of that kind. I am basing my statement on a return brought down by the minister himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
with his long parliamentary experience knows that he is not stating any point of order, but let that pass. I stated that he was basing his figures on an estimate of his own. While it is true that the department has a certain scale of fees for certain services rendered, nevertheless these doctors have all been advised, or if they have not all yet received the advice they will in the near future, that their accounts for the year must not exceed a certain amount. I may say for the information of the hon. member that a certain doctor was appointed by myself after this government took office, and as the accounts he sent in were too big his attention was drawn to it; still they came in too big, and his services were therefore dispensed with and another doctor was appointed in his place. When the hon. member makes the statement that this change is going to cost some $900 as compared with some $400 for the previous year, he is making a statement that can be substantiated 
only when the returns for the year are in, showing what the services actually cost. When the hon. member makes a definite statement that the costs will be so and so, and that it will cost the country so much more, he is making a statement which, I submit, is unfair. He is basing his statement upon figures before him and not upon accounts rendered.

I am basing my statement upon a return made by the minister. I am pointing out some glaring instances which my hon. friend cannot get over, and which returns this year or next year or any other year will not alter. To call a doctor in the town to treat an Indian in Shelburne, where Doctor Churchill resides, would cost only $3, but to call Doctor Herbin would cost $19. Any information the minister can bring down will not change the figures. The minister says there is some limit placed upon the fees charged by the doctors. What limit was placed upon Doctor Herbin when he took office with regard to his salary or emoluments?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. member had
been listening carefully he would have heard my statement that instructions had been sent out to the different doctors throughout Canada-if they have not yet received them, they will-to the effect that their accounts must not exceed a certain amount for the year. I am not at the present time in a position to say whether or not instructions went out to the doctor mentioned by my hon. friend. The figure will be set at such and such an amount, and this country will not have to pay the sum mentioned by my hon. friend, or anything like it.
Will the minister be good enough to tell me, when his estimates are again under consideration, whether a sum has been set for Doctor Herbin's services, and if so when, and the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that the
figure has been set at $20 a month.

I wish to put on record
a question I asked and the answer thereto as it appears in Hansard for the present session at page 389:
Is the present incumbent on salary, if so, how much, and if paid on a fee basis what is the scale?
The answer is:
The present incumbent is employed on the "call system" and is paid for services rendered on the basis of the department's schedule of fees quoted in part as follows: Visits-within 3 miles, $3 per call; outside 3 miles, $1 per mile one way, to cover transportation, professional attendance and supply of ordinary

Supply-Indian Affairs
remedies to all patients attended on trip; office consultations, $2 to include supply of ordinary remedies; surgical operations, as detailed in the schedule, etc.
In that answer there is not one word about a limit of any kind or description.
Mr. DONNELLY; It seems utterly ridiculous to limit the amount paid to k doctor each month. Is the government going to prevent the Indians from being sick or if they are sick will the government let them die without calling in a doctor? I did some work for the Indians two years ago, and I had some experience in this practice of cutting down fees. The department did not wish to spend too much. I have been called out to see Indians suffering from pneumonia, and then the Indian agent would tell the person in charge of the patient when I could be called in again. The result was that probably I would never hear from them again, or would be called to write out a death certificate. If the Indians are going to be sick they have to send for a doctor; the government or nobody else can say when they are going to be sick, how often they are going to be sick or how often they may need a doctor.
Oh, this government can.

Oh, can they? The
whole thing seems ridiculous.

Can the minister tell
me why the services of Doctor J. B. Cloutier of the Roseau River Indian reserve were dispensed with? Was it for the reason expressed by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, namely that when a Conservative government takes office all the Grits are thrown out?
Mr. MURPHY; I did not hear the hon. member's question.

Why in the month of
January 1931 were the services of Doctor J. B. Cloutier dispensed with?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed Doctor
Cloutier was paid on the call system.
I believe that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I said a minute ago,
wffien I received a recommendation from a colleague or from some one in whom I had confidence that the services should be performed by a certain doctor or individual, I acted on that recommendation. While I have not the particulars before me, I assume that was what was done in reference to Doctor Cloutier.

Will the minister tell
me that one of his colleagues in the house from the province of Manitoba has told him that another doctor should replace Doctor Cloutier? Would he show me any correspondence to that effect from one of his colleagues in the government, or from one of the back benchers, in which class the Minister of Agriculture has qualified himself? Did such a man give him a letter, or ask him to dismiss Doctor Cloutier?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have stated as clearly as my English would allow that I acted on the recommendation of a colleague, or one in whose judgment I had confidence. I have no letter from a colleague or a member of this house before me to-night in regard to that particular individual. I have confidence, however, in the judgment of a great many men who are not members of this house, and are not my colleagues.

I think the minister
would have fewer questions to answer if he did not take the recommendations of his friends who are not in the house, who have no first hand knowledge, and who probably make accusations which cannot be proven. Is it correct that the Indian agent when buying supplies or necessities for the Indians asks different people to give figures, or written tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Generally speaking that is correct, but in isolated sections there may be only one source of supply.

I am not speaking of
isolated sections. It seems that certain merchants in certain towns are on preferred lists. The Indian agents ask those people to tender or to give a figure on supplies needed by the Indians. Can the minister inform me, so I may pass the information on to the merchants in my district, what procedure a man has to take to be on the preferred list?
Mr. Chairman-

I should like to have
an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. The agent buys
supplies for the Indians in isolated communities from those w-ho can supply or are close at hand. Certain of the larger supplies, such as bacon, tea and so on, are bought in wholesale quantities. With regard to some particular friends of his who desired to supply goods to the Indians, possibly my hon. friend had better inform them that when he can make representations such as he desires no doubt they will be carried out.
Supply-Indian Affairs

I think the minister will admit that instructions are sent out to the Indian agents to ask certain people to give a price on certain commodities needed for the Indians. Do those instructions come from the minister, or from his deputy, or from a local political organization? I want to get into the ring myself; that is all I am looking for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
has answered his own question, he seems so familiar with a procedure which possibly he has followed himself in the past ten years I fancy that the method that is being followed now is practically the same method as has been followed for the past ten years.

For the minister's information, I may saj' that I have been a member of this house since December 26, 1921, and I have yet to ask for the dismissal of one person on political grounds. I hope he will remember that and let the officials in my district alone. No politician has the right to take the bread out of the mouth of any man, whether he be blue or green.
Or red.
Or red.
Will the minister be good enough to give me the papers in connection with the removal of the Indian doctor at Shelburne? I moved for them some time ago, but they have not yet been brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall be pleased to have them laid on the table as soon as possible.
Including the letter which limits the amount of pay Doctor Herbin is to get.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think I stated
a letter had been sent to this particular person.
I understand so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I stated I was informed
that a sum had been set not to exceed S20 a month, or $240 per year.
The doctor does not know it yet?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He may.
He will get a rude awakening.

Will the minister also
let me have the correspondence in regard to the dismissal of Doctor Cloutier of the Roseau River Indian reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any correspondence which can be properly brought down I will certainly have laid on the table.

How does it
happen that these individual Indians have accounts with the merchants of. the various towns, if supplies are bought under tender by the agent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Tenders are asked for by the department when the goods are purchased. If an individual Indian desires to purchase goods from a certain merchant, the agent simply takes upon himself the responsibility to pay the account, if he can obtain sufficient money for the purpose out of the proceeds of the crop.
I have in mind an Indian purchasing something on his own account, apart from the agent altogether. In that case what portion of the money does he get under his personal control?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He may purchase his goods wherever he likes, the same as any other individual, provided he has the cash.
Does he get some from the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He gets it either out of the proceeds of his crop, his treaty money, or the interest on his band fund.

If an appointment is made by the Civil Service Commission of one of the four candidates for the Cacouna Indian agency, will the minister be ready to accept it at once, or will he postpone its acceptance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It will be a matter for
consideration.

On September 5, 1930,
Howard Brothers, supplying Indians, were notified by the superintendent or Indian agent at Fredericton to discontinue doing so. Will the minister let me know at a later date on whose recommendation the Indian agent was so instructed; and if tenders were asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall be pleased to give the hon. member any information I can obtain in regard to the matter.

In connection with the question of the purchase of coal on the Blackfoot reserve, I should be glad if the minister can explain to the committee why it is that in the case of fuel supplies for the agency tenders were invited from only two firms-one of them, Mr. William McConnell, not a coal dealer at all, while the other, the

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
Midland Collieries, is a long distance from Gleichen and from the reserve itself-when there are actually in the town no less than three regular coal dealers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no first hand knowledge as to whether Mr. McConnell is a coal dealer or not, and no doubt the hon. member has fuller information than I have, but I have before me some of his account forms, which are headed; "William McConnell, Coal and Grain, Oils, Greases and Gasoline". This would convey to my mind at least that he is a dealer in coal. The Midland Collieries, I am informed, is one of the largest operators of coal mines in Alberta.
Why are special persons only invited to tender? Is that a proper practice to follow?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has been the practice in the department, I am informed, for many years.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the sittings of the committee raised some question as to a report that appeared in this evening's papers. I am bound to say that my attention was directed to this report, and probably about the time the right hon. gentleman was speaking in the committee I was speaking to the chairman, He told me that the committee has not completed its report, that it is still meeting, that no report has been agreed upon, and that no information was given to the press by the chairman or the secretary of the committee. Obviously I have not interviewed the various members of the committee, for reasons that are apparent. I should like to assure the house that the information was not given to the press by either the chairman or the secretary of the committee, and the report is not yet completed.
That is the information I have received since the house met at eight o'clock, and I immediately convey it to the house because I think this house is entitled to receive information with regard to the report of any committee before it is given to the press.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
Monday, May 9, 1932.
